title: DNS Server Zone Transfer Monitoring
exclusions: Detects Windows DNS Server Analytical IXFR/AXFR requests received and responses sent (Microsoft event IDs 266/267/270/271) whose exact DNS server, zone, transfer type/direction, and peer IP do not match a currently effective governed partner row. It does not assert that an inbound request succeeded, that an outbound response contained a complete zone, that `RCODE=0` proves all records transferred, or that an unauthorized event is malicious. It does not cover request-out/response-in activity by secondaries (265/268/269/272), NOTIFY (273/274), DNS queries unrelated to transfer, packet payload inspection, TCP session completion, transfer-policy/configuration drift, zone enumeration through ordinary queries, non-Windows DNS, cloud-managed DNS, encrypted DNS, DNSSEC validity, or data exfiltration over DNS. Analytical logging can be absent, delayed, filtered, malformed, or too expensive; missing telemetry is not proof that no transfer occurred. The exact source type/index, 30-minute closed window, five-minute delay, lookup schema, and alert-on-any-unknown rule are local contracts rather than Microsoft or Splunk defaults. The UC changes no zone, transfer permission, policy, NS record, secondary, service, firewall, or response control and makes no regulatory-attestation claim.
evidence: After deployment, retain the authoritative Windows DNS server/zone inventory; same-time `Get-DnsServerZone`, primary-zone `SecureSecondaries`/`SecondaryServers`, NS records, and zone-transfer policies; the version-controlled `dns_zone_transfer_partners.csv` revision and approval; effective DNS Analytical collection/filter and Splunk parsing configuration; raw XML/ETW events 266/267/270/271; independent source-health output; saved search `windows_dns_unauthorized_zone_transfer_peer`, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and result rows; dashboard/alert revisions; bounded exceptions; network/runtime corroboration; incident disposition; and dated positive, negative, lookup-boundary, source-direction, duplicate, late-arrival, malformed-field, and policy-change tests. Preserve server, source, provider, event ID, transfer type/direction, zone, peer IP, RCODE, transaction ID, record identity, event/index times, lookup policy, and reason. This documentation-only review created no Windows DNS, transfer, Splunk, dashboard, alert, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated index with fixed event/dispatch time, ingest one `msdns:analytical` event 270 with `dest=dns01.example`, `Source=192.0.2.44`, `Zone=example.test`, `EventRecordID=7001`, and an effective lookup containing no exact `(dns01.example,example.test,AXFR,inbound_request,192.0.2.44)` row. Expect exactly one result with `transfer_type=AXFR`, `transfer_direction=inbound_request`, `peer_ip=192.0.2.44`, and `authorization_reason=no_exact_effective_partner`. Separately ingest event 267 with `Destination=192.0.2.45`, the same zone, and `RCODE=0`; expect an `IXFR/outbound_response` result without claiming transfer completeness.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Use one active lookup row with exact normalized server, zone, type, direction, peer, `authorized=yes`, integer inclusive `valid_from_epoch`, and exclusive `valid_until_epoch`; the matching event must return zero rows. Also require zero rows for event IDs 265/268/269/272/273/274, events outside `msdns:analytical`, malformed or missing server/zone/peer/event identity, events outside the closed window, and an exact partner at the inclusive start. An entry at its exclusive expiry, `authorized` other than yes, wildcard/blank identity, mismatched direction/type/zone/server, duplicate active lookup rows, or noninteger time must not authorize; the main result or companion policy/source-health search must surface the defect. Replay of one EventRecordID must not produce two findings.

dataSources: Primary source is the Windows DNS Server Analytical ETW channel collected and normalized by Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows as `index=dns`, `sourcetype=msdns:analytical`. Microsoft documents event 266 as IXFR request in (`Source` peer), 267 as IXFR response out (`Destination` peer and `RCODE`), 270 as AXFR request in, and 271 as AXFR response out. Required normalized fields are DNS server (`dest`, `Computer`, or `host`), integer `EventCode`, `Zone`/`QNAME`/`query`, direction-specific `Source` or `Destination`, and `EventRecordID`/`RecordNumber`; retain `XID`, `RCODE`, `ZoneScope`, `InterfaceIP`, provider, `_time`, and `_indextime`. `dns_zone_transfer_partners.csv` is deployment-owned policy sourced from approved zone configuration, NS/secondary design, and transfer policies—not observed traffic.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) for Windows DNS Analytical collection/normalization to `msdns:analytical` and Network Resolution fields. A local security app owns lookup `dns_zone_transfer_partners`, saved search `windows_dns_unauthorized_zone_transfer_peer`, policy/source-health searches, dashboard, fixtures, bounded suppression, and alert routing. No premium app is required.
spl:
index=dns sourcetype="msdns:analytical" EventCode IN (266,267,270,271) earliest=-35m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval dns_server=lower(coalesce(nullif(trim(Computer),""),nullif(trim(ComputerName),""),nullif(trim(host),""),nullif(trim(dest),""))), event_id=tonumber(EventCode), zone=lower(rtrim(coalesce(nullif(trim(Zone),""),nullif(trim(QNAME),""),nullif(trim(query),"")),".")), transfer_type=case(in(event_id,266,267),"IXFR",in(event_id,270,271),"AXFR"), transfer_direction=case(in(event_id,266,270),"inbound_request",in(event_id,267,271),"outbound_response"), peer_ip=lower(trim(case(in(event_id,266,270),coalesce(Source,src,src_ip),in(event_id,267,271),coalesce(Destination,dest_ip)))), event_record_id=trim(tostring(coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber))), transaction_id=tostring(coalesce(XID,transaction_id,"not_extracted")), response_code=tostring(coalesce(RCODE,reply_code_id,"not_applicable"))
| where len(dns_server)>0 AND isnotnull(event_id) AND event_id=floor(event_id) AND len(zone)>0 AND len(peer_ip)>0 AND len(event_record_id)>0
| eval event_identity=dns_server."|".source."|".event_record_id
| dedup event_identity
| lookup dns_zone_transfer_partners dns_server zone transfer_type transfer_direction peer_ip OUTPUT authorized as policy_authorized valid_from_epoch valid_until_epoch partner_id policy_id
| eval valid_from_epoch=tonumber(valid_from_epoch), valid_until_epoch=tonumber(valid_until_epoch), policy_match=if(policy_authorized="yes" AND isnotnull(valid_from_epoch) AND valid_from_epoch=floor(valid_from_epoch) AND isnotnull(valid_until_epoch) AND valid_until_epoch=floor(valid_until_epoch) AND valid_from_epoch<=_time AND _time<valid_until_epoch AND len(partner_id)>0 AND len(policy_id)>0,1,0), authorization_reason=if(policy_match=1,"authorized","no_exact_effective_partner")
| where policy_match=0
| eval use_case="UC-1.2.96", first_seen=strftime(_time,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
| table _time dns_server source event_id transfer_type transfer_direction zone peer_ip response_code transaction_id ZoneScope InterfaceIP event_record_id authorization_reason partner_id policy_id first_seen _indextime use_case
| sort 0 dns_server zone transfer_type transfer_direction peer_ip _time
description: Detects inbound Windows DNS Server IXFR/AXFR requests and outbound transfer responses involving a peer that lacks an exact, currently effective authorization for the DNS server, zone, transfer type, and direction. It uses Microsoft-documented Analytical event IDs and direction-specific peer fields while retaining RCODE and transaction context without equating a request or response with a completed zone disclosure.
value: A DNS zone can expose hostnames, service roles, and delegation structure, while secondary service legitimately depends on controlled transfers. Matching every observed transfer interaction to approved server/zone/peer policy reduces the time needed to identify reconnaissance attempts, stale secondary configuration, and unintended outbound paths without treating all AXFR/IXFR traffic as hostile or claiming that an informational event proves successful data delivery.
implementation: Enable and benchmark the Windows DNS Server Analytical channel on every governed authoritative/secondary server, collect it as `msdns:analytical`, and validate events 266/267/270/271 and payload fields on every supported build. Generate a reviewed, exact partner lookup from zone transfer settings, secondaries/NS records, virtualization instance/zone scope, and transfer policies, with effective times and no wildcards. Save the SPL as `windows_dns_unauthorized_zone_transfer_peer`, run it five minutes after each closed 30-minute window, and alert on any unapproved interaction. Correlate request/response pairs, RCODE, TCP/network evidence, current zone policy, and service owner before asserting exposure or changing DNS.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows DNS — Zone Transfer Governance`: show expected DNS-server Analytical freshness, malformed records, lookup duplicates/expiry, and zones lacking policy first. Then show unauthorized inbound requests and outbound responses separately by AXFR/IXFR, zone, server, peer, RCODE, and count. Provide a table with event/record IDs, XID, zone scope, interface, exact policy result, event/index times, and partner owner; trends over 24 hours and 30 days; and drilldowns to raw ETW/XML, matching request/response, same-time DNS Manager/PowerShell settings, transfer policy, NS/secondary records, firewall/packet evidence, and incident. Geographic enrichment may be shown only for validated public peer IPs and must not imply actor location.
schema: Windows DNS Server Analytical zone-transfer events plus exact effective partner policy
dataModelAcceleration: The add-on maps `msdns:analytical` to Network_Resolution, but the generic accelerated dataset is not asserted to preserve Microsoft event ID, inbound-versus-outbound transfer direction, `Zone`, `ZoneScope`, `Source`/`Destination`, XID, RCODE, EventRecordID, or exact policy identity. Therefore the primary detector uses raw normalized events. A purpose-built summary is acceptable only after parity tests preserve every identity, direction, policy/effective-time decision, duplicate, and malformed/source-health state.

knownFalsePositives:
A result is a true policy nonmatch for a documented transfer event; it can reflect stale governance, legitimate transition, or refused reconnaissance rather than successful theft.

1. **New or renumbered secondary** — A planned secondary can begin requesting before its exact peer IP/effective policy reaches Splunk. Verify change, zone, server, transfer mode, secondary identity, IP ownership, NS/secondary settings, and lookup deployment. Fix ordering; do not grant a wildcard subnet.

2. **DNS migration, cutover, or disaster recovery** — Old and new primaries/secondaries may overlap temporarily. Require exact zone/server/peer/direction/type, inclusive start, exclusive expiry, owner, and rollback. Remove retired paths after SOA/serial and service validation.

3. **Load balancer, NAT, anycast, or multi-homed source identity** — The DNS server may observe a translated or alternate address rather than the management inventory address. Validate packet path and destination-specific address; authorize only the address actually expected at that server, not an entire broad range.

4. **Approved vulnerability scanner or DNS audit** — A scanner may send AXFR/IXFR requests to prove they are refused. Event 266/270 is request evidence, not transfer success. Confirm scanner owner, target list, test time, and response/network evidence; retain the event even if notification is suppressed.

5. **Rejected internet or internal reconnaissance** — An unauthorized request that the server refuses is not a false event. Classify it as attempted transfer, verify RCODE/response and policy, and severity-route by exposure and recurrence rather than closing it as a false positive.

6. **Transfer-policy or NS design differs from the static lookup** — `TransferToZoneNameServer`, `TransferToSecureServers`, server/zone-level policies, and virtualization instances can produce legitimate peers missed by a naive list. Generate policy from approved effective configuration and preserve its derivation; observed traffic alone cannot authorize itself.

7. **Duplicate ETW collection or replay** — Restored ETL/EVTX, checkpoint reset, or dual collectors can repeat a record. The search deduplicates exact server/source/record identity in-window; source health must still identify and correct the route.

8. **Malformed or missing direction-specific fields** — A parser/build change can leave `Source`, `Destination`, or `Zone` null. Such events are source-health defects and cannot authorize or prove absence. Requalify the exact Windows/add-on version before changing coalesces.

**Safe notification suppression:** preserve the base result and use a post-result exception keyed by exact `dns_server,zone,transfer_type,transfer_direction,peer_ip,event_id`, with numeric inclusive start, exclusive expiry, owner, approver, ticket, and reason. Reject wildcards, open-ended entries, traffic-derived authorization, and suppression of missing/malformed source or policy data.
detectionType: Exact effective-policy mismatch for Microsoft DNS zone-transfer events
hardware: Windows Server systems running Microsoft DNS Server with the Analytical channel available and qualified for collection. Non-Windows authoritative servers, managed DNS services, recursive-only resolvers, appliances, network-only sensors, and secondaries whose request-out/response-in activity is the monitoring objective require a separate source/direction contract.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against primary Microsoft Windows DNS Analytical event and DNS zone/transfer-policy PowerShell documentation plus Splunk Microsoft Windows add-on source-type/CIM field documentation; event payloads, ETW collection, server/zone/partner inventory, policy derivation, effective-time lookup, SPL, fixtures, thresholds, source health, alerting, and production behavior were specified but not executed or Microsoft/Splunk/DNS/network/security-operations SME signed

cost.search_load_notes: The primary search reads four event IDs over one closed 30-minute window and performs one exact lookup. The ingest cost can be high because DNS Analytical logging records broad server activity; measure QPS, filter support, ETW loss, and add-on parsing without dropping transfer events.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and event meaning

Assign Windows DNS, IPAM/network, Splunk collection/content, security-response, and zone-owner roles. Inventory every in-scope DNS server, virtualization instance, primary/secondary/stub/forwarder role, zone and scope, master/secondary path, NS record, `SecureSecondaries` value, `SecondaryServers`, NOTIFY configuration, server- and zone-level transfer policy, NAT/load-balancer path, and owner. Define stable lowercase DNS-server and zone names and canonical peer IP strings. The lookup is approved configuration policy; never populate it automatically from observed traffic.

Microsoft documents DNS Server Analytical IDs 265-274. This detector deliberately uses only 266 (IXFR request in), 267 (IXFR response out), 270 (AXFR request in), and 271 (AXFR response out), because those events expose the remote peer from the monitored server's receiving/request or sending/response perspective. Event 266/270 proves a request reached the DNS service, not that it was accepted. Event 267/271 proves a response event was emitted, not packet delivery, TCP completion, completeness, or recipient use. Preserve `RCODE` and network evidence before claiming successful disclosure.

Install and qualify a supported `Splunk_TA_windows`. The collection identity needs the tested local rights required to consume the DNS Analytical ETW channel and forward data; it needs no permission to edit zones, policies, records, secondaries, service state, or firewall. Search roles need access to `index=dns`; lookup editors must be a smaller governed role than search users. DNS payloads can expose internal names, addresses, and topology, so restrict raw searches and exports.

## Step 1 — Enable, benchmark, and collect Analytical events

Microsoft states DNS audit logging is enabled by default, while Analytical logging tracks send/receive activity and can affect high-query-rate servers. Enable it first in a production-representative lab, then canary servers, and measure DNS latency, CPU, QPS, ETW event loss, channel behavior, forwarder load, and ingest volume. Do not cite one historic performance percentage as a guarantee for current hardware/builds.

Use the add-on's documented DNS Analytical collection path and confirm `sourcetype=msdns:analytical`. The exact input mechanism can vary by supported add-on version; follow that release's configuration rather than inventing a generic classic WinEventLog stanza for an Analytic channel. Verify effective deployment, provider GUID/channel, enabled state, buffers, filters, index routing, parsing tier, and time synchronization. On Splunk Cloud, collection runs on customer-managed Windows infrastructure, not the managed search tier.

Generate controlled, nonsecret AXFR and IXFR lab transactions. For each supported Windows Server build, compare the source event with Splunk and verify IDs and documented payloads: 266/270 use `Source`; 267/271 use `Destination` and include `RCODE`; all carry zone context and transaction ID in Microsoft's templates. Confirm the add-on's actual aliases (`dest`, `src`, `query`, `transaction_id`, and others) rather than assuming every release uses the same case. Preserve raw field names for forensic parity.

Maintain a companion source-health search that reports expected server missing, stale latest event/canary, wrong source type, malformed event ID, missing direction-specific peer, empty zone, missing record identity, future event time, excessive indexing delay, duplicate route/replay, parser version drift, ETW loss/buffer warning, and sudden volume collapse. A DNS server can have no zone transfers for long periods, so configuration inventory or a safe scheduled canary is required to distinguish quiet service from absent telemetry.

## Step 2 — Govern exact transfer authorization

Create `dns_zone_transfer_partners.csv` with exact fields `dns_server,zone,transfer_type,transfer_direction,peer_ip,authorized,valid_from_epoch,valid_until_epoch,partner_id,policy_id,owner,ticket`. One row grants only one normalized server/zone/type/direction/peer combination. `valid_from_epoch` is inclusive and `valid_until_epoch` exclusive, both integer UTC epoch seconds. Require `authorized=yes`, nonempty partner/policy IDs, owner, approver, reason, source-of-truth reference, and review date. Reject wildcard servers/zones/IPs, CIDR-as-text matches, blank fields, overlapping duplicate active rows, invalid IPs, end-before-start, and open-ended emergency entries.

Derive each row from the effective Windows DNS design, not merely `Get-DnsServerZone`. Microsoft documents `SecureSecondaries` modes `NoTransfer`, `TransferAnyServer`, `TransferToZoneNameServer`, and `TransferToSecureServers`, plus explicit `SecondaryServers`. Also inventory `Get-DnsServerZoneTransferPolicy` at server and zone levels, NS address resolution, virtualization instances, zone scopes, NAT, and multi-homing. A setting that permits transfer to NS servers still needs deterministic approved peer addresses for this monitoring policy. `TransferAnyServer` is a configuration-risk finding and must not become `peer_ip=*`.

Review the lookup after any DNS/IPAM/NS/secondary/NAT/zone/policy/server change and at least quarterly. Deployment must be atomic across the search tier. A policy-health search should detect duplicates, invalid times, wildcard/blank identities, unknown servers/zones, retired peers, lookup deployment mismatch, and configuration-to-lookup drift. Policy failure must not silently authorize an event.

## Step 3 — Create and understand the primary SPL

Save the sidecar SPL as `windows_dns_unauthorized_zone_transfer_peer` and schedule it every 30 minutes with a five-minute delay. `earliest=-35m@m latest=-5m@m` creates a closed, nonoverlapping event-time window. Measure p99 ETW-to-index delay; move both bounds together if needed and reconcile late arrivals separately.

The base search selects only `msdns:analytical` and four Microsoft-documented IDs. It normalizes server, numeric event ID, lowercase zone without a trailing dot, type, direction, direction-specific peer, record identity, XID, and RCODE. Required identity failures are rejected from trusted policy comparison and must appear in source health. Exact server/source/record deduplication prevents a checkpoint replay from creating duplicate findings while preserving the routing defect for health monitoring.

The lookup key includes every authorization dimension. A row authorizes only when `authorized=yes`, both effective times are integers, event time is at or after start and before expiry, and partner/policy IDs are present. No row, expired/future row, malformed row, or mismatched key becomes `no_exact_effective_partner`. Lookup duplicates must be blocked by the policy gate because an SPL lookup returning one arbitrary row is not a safe conflict resolver.

Do not replace this with `tstats count by src,dest`. Generic Network Resolution fields are useful for DNS analytics, but the policy decision needs event ID, exact transfer direction, zone, XID/RCODE, record identity, and effective lookup provenance. Likewise, events 6001/6002 are not the Microsoft-documented zone-transfer Analytical IDs used here and must not be assigned AXFR/IXFR meanings without a separate primary source.

## Step 4 — Validate event directions, policy boundaries, and Windows behavior

Run the exact controls against an isolated index and temporary lookup with fixed `now()`/event times. Test all four IDs independently; assert that request-in uses Source and response-out uses Destination. Test trailing-dot/case normalization, IPv4 and the qualified IPv6 representation, exact zone/server/type/direction differences, same record number on different servers, duplicate replay, missing fields, noninteger IDs/times, window boundaries, late arrival, inclusive policy start, exclusive expiry, overlapping rows, and unknown lookup deployment.

In an isolated DNS lab, configure one disposable primary and approved secondary for a nonproduction zone. Capture a permitted IXFR and AXFR where supported, then a request from an unlisted peer. Compare raw Analytical events with DNS Manager and same-time PowerShell:

```powershell
Get-DnsServerZone -ComputerName dns01
Get-DnsServerZoneTransferPolicy -ComputerName dns01
Get-DnsServerZoneTransferPolicy -ComputerName dns01 -ZoneName example.test
```

Inspect primary-zone settings, `SecureSecondaries`, explicit secondary servers, NS records, SOA/serial, zone scope/virtualization instance, and policies. Use an approved DNS client to issue transfer requests; do not expose a production zone, relax production transfer permissions, publish secrets, or modify firewalls merely to create a positive. Sanitize fixture zone names and packet data.

For an inbound unauthorized request, verify whether a response event follows and inspect RCODE plus packet/TCP evidence. For an outbound response, verify peer, zone, serial/transfer behavior, and receiving secondary state. Document that one event cannot prove the full zone crossed the network. Keep `status=draft` until DNS and Splunk owners validate fields, collection performance, partner policy, controls, source health, alert delivery, dashboard, and response.

## Step 5 — Triage, respond, and preserve evidence

Alert on any result, but severity depends on direction, response/RCODE, zone sensitivity, peer ownership, exposure, recurrence, configuration, and corroborated network transfer. An internet request that was refused differs from an unapproved outbound response with apparent success. Alert text must say `Unapproved Windows DNS zone-transfer interaction` rather than `zone stolen`.

Responder sequence:
1. Validate source/type, raw ID/payload, server, zone, type, direction, peer, record/XID, times, duplicate state, and source health.
2. Compare exact effective lookup revision and its derivation with current DNS primary-zone settings, NS/secondary inventory, transfer policies, virtualization instance/zone scope, NAT, and change ticket.
3. Correlate request and response events by server/zone/peer/type/XID/time; inspect RCODE and packet/firewall telemetry where legally and technically available.
4. Identify the peer through authoritative IPAM/asset/cloud/NAT records; do not rely on GeoIP or reverse DNS as identity proof.
5. Determine whether the event is a refused scan, stale legitimate secondary, configuration drift, migration, test, or likely unintended disclosure; assess zone content and user impact.
6. Follow DNS incident/change procedures. Preserve current state before modifying permissions, policies, NS records, or secondaries.

Never automatically block a peer, disable zone transfer, change `SecureSecondaries`, remove a secondary/NS record, stop DNS, delete a zone, rotate records, or isolate a server from this result alone. An automatic change can break authoritative service or replication. Verify recovery with current configuration, a permitted secondary transfer/serial check, a refused unapproved test where authorized, continued source health, and absence of unexplained outbound responses.

Retain artifacts named in `evidence` under local security/privacy policy. Zone names and packet data can reveal internal topology; limit raw access and ticket copying. Apply suppression only after the base policy mismatch and only with the exact bounded contract in `knownFalsePositives`.

## Step 6 — Troubleshoot without authorizing uncertainty

- **No `msdns:analytical` events:** verify DNS role/build, Analytical enabled state, add-on-supported collection method, ETW provider/buffers, forwarder service, queues, index, parser, time range, and role. No rows do not prove no transfer.
- **Wrong IDs such as 6001/6002:** remove undocumented transfer labels and validate against Microsoft's current DNS logging table and raw provider manifest for the exact build.
- **Zone or peer is null:** compare raw event payload, direction, add-on version, extraction case, source type, and props. Route malformed data to health; do not use host IP or regex over rendered text as a silent substitute.
- **Every event is unauthorized:** confirm lookup deployment/ACL, exact normalized keys, trailing dots, direction, type, event-time effective interval, NAT address, and duplicate/invalid policy rows.
- **Expected request has no response:** inspect server policy, RCODE in other events, TCP/firewall path, packet data, rate limits, and DNS logs. Do not infer refusal or success from absence while source health is uncertain.
- **Response has RCODE 0:** treat as stronger corroboration, not proof of complete delivery. Correlate TCP/packet and receiving-secondary serial/state.
- **Analytical logging harms capacity:** measure and tune supported ETW filters/buffers or use an approved network sensor while preserving all 266/267/270/271 events. Never drop one direction silently.
- **Duplicate findings:** inspect EventRecordID, `_indextime`, ETL/EVTX replay, WEF/direct routes, and lookup duplicates. Correct source/policy rather than broad deduplication.
- **CIM search lacks transfer direction:** expected; use raw normalized events for this policy contract.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for full copy requests of your whole DNS zone so you can see transfers that are not in your list of real secondaries before someone walks away with a map of your names.
